candidates.title: Someone makes Ted a BELIEVE sign
candidates.detail: Ted skips the team's New Year's Eve parties for a quiet night with his ex-wife Michelle and their son Henry. He admits he feels adrift. When he comes back upstairs she has painted him a fresh BELIEVE sign out of Henry's school-project supplies, with a note. Multiple recaps describe the reversal plainly: the man who spent three seasons handing that word to other people is on the receiving end of it. Maps to the project's existing William James chapter — precursive faith, believing in advance of the evidence — because the sign only means anything when the evidence is thin.
candidates.moment: Ted comes back up from a long, honest talk to find a hand-painted sign waiting, made from a kid's leftover craft supplies, with a short note beside it.

candidates.title: Voltaire, or as Jamie has it, Voltron
candidates.detail: At the hospital, Jamie tries to talk Rebecca out of her own perfectionism and offers a maxim to the effect that perfect is the opposite of good — crediting it to 'Voltron' rather than Voltaire. The underlying maxim is real and is genuinely associated with Voltaire: 'le mieux est l'ennemi du bien.' What makes it a good card is that Voltaire himself presented it as borrowed — he cites it as an Italian proverb ('Il meglio e l'inimico del bene') in Questions sur l'Encyclopedie (1770) and repeats it in the poem La Begueule (1772) as the saying of a wise Italian. Montesquieu had written something close in his Pensees decades earlier. So a garbled attribution sits on top of a maxim that was already a second-hand attribution — the same shape as the show's Whitman sign. FLAG: the wording of Jamie's line comes from reviewers' paraphrase, not a transcript; the card must paraphrase, not quote.
candidates.moment: In a hospital corridor, Jamie tells Rebecca she is chasing something perfect instead of accepting something good, and confidently credits the wrong name.

candidates.title: The title is two songs stitched together
candidates.detail: The episode title folds Duke Ellington's standard 'Don't Get Around Much Anymore' into House of Pain's 'Jump Around.' Ellington recorded the tune as an instrumental called 'Never No Lament' in May 1940; Bob Russell added the lyric in 1942 and it became a hit — a song about a man who no longer goes out. 'Jump Around' (House of Pain, 1992, produced by DJ Muggs of Cypress Hill) is the opposite: the song stadiums play to get everyone off their seats. It is also the song Roy's knee gives out to. The joke and the ache are the same joke: a man who used to jump around.
candidates.moment: The title card, read against the dance-floor scene it is named for.

candidates.title: Roy's knee, again
candidates.detail: Roy dances with Jamie at the vodka launch and his knee goes. The knee is the show's oldest running injury — it is what forced him out of the game in the first season — and here it takes him out of a party rather than a match. Reviewers read the scene as the season's clearest statement of the aging-athlete thread that has followed Roy since he stopped playing.

candidates.title: The encourager admits he is adrift
candidates.detail: Ted tells Michelle he has been feeling adrift and is unsure he is getting it right with the team, including the coach he suspended. Reviews across the board single this out as the episode's most honest material and note the picture it paints: lonely, not settled in the new job, quietly struggling underneath the optimism. It is the counterweight the show has always needed for the BELIEVE sign, and it arrives in the same scene as the sign.
candidates.moment: Over a slow pub evening, Ted says out loud that he does not know if he is doing the right thing.

candidates.title: Understanding without getting back together
candidates.detail: Michelle talks about how lonely she was after the divorce and encourages Ted to start dating again, pointing him at a stage manager he has already met. Reviewers describe the scene as a rare screen version of two divorced people reaching real understanding without that understanding pointing toward reconciliation, and the note she leaves him reportedly says as much: divorce is not a failure. FLAG: recaps differ on the exact wording of the note and on how much detail she gives about her own relationship since — paraphrase only, and do not assert specifics about who she is with now.
candidates.moment: Two people who used to be married talk honestly about the years since, and neither one is angling to fix it.

candidates.title: The book in Alice's flat
candidates.detail: In the domestic scene at Alice Chilton's home, her girlfriend is reading Anais Nin's novel A Spy in the House of Love (1954) — a book about a woman living several incompatible versions of herself and dreading being found out. It lands on the same character the episode is about: Alice is one person at home and a guarded, hard-to-know person around the team. It also continues an Anais Nin thread the previous episode started. FLAG: sourced to two reviews; I could not find a third or a production source.

candidates.title: Michelle is writing about Mark Twain
candidates.detail: Michelle is revealed to be a writer, working on a book about Mark Twain's time in London — and Ted uses the book as a way to change the subject when she asks about his personal life. Twain really did spend extended stretches in London in the early 1870s. FLAG: sources agree she is writing on Twain abroad but differ slightly on framing (London specifically vs. Twain in Europe).

candidates.title: Back at practice, like nothing happened
candidates.detail: Alice, suspended in the previous episode, turns up anyway after being talked into it at home. Ted finds her at the party, wishes her a happy new year and tells her he will see her at practice as if nothing happened. It is the show's usual position on punishment — the sanction ends when it ends, and the person is not made to carry it afterward — which maps to the project's existing chapter on forgiveness and treating people as full moral agents.
candidates.moment: Ted arrives late to the team's celebration and settles the suspension in one short exchange.

candidates.title: Advocated for, without being asked
candidates.detail: Gemma reassures Alice that the team does not dislike her, they just do not know her. Then Lizzie lets slip that Gemma had already told the team about Alice's worries. The kindness and the betrayal are the same act — someone explained you to a room you were not in. It is a sharper piece of ethics than the episode's romantic misunderstandings, and reviewers noticed the contrast.
candidates.moment: A reassurance lands well until a third party mentions where it came from.

candidates.title: Apple Tartt
candidates.detail: Jamie returns — Phil Dunster guesting, and blond again — to launch a vodka brand called Apple Tartt, with dancers and an Adam-and-Eve-themed entrance.
